cognate: Russ. свекор = Gk ἑκυρός = Ved. śváśura- (*swéḱuros); свекруха/свекровь = ἑκυρά = śvaśrū́- (*sweḱrúh₂); деверь = δαήρ (Il. 24.769) = devṛ́- (*dayh₂wḗr); золовушки (context line, золовка < *zъlъva) = γάλως (gen. pl. γαλόων, Il. 24.769) (*ǵl̥h₂ōws); the δαήρ, γάλως/золовка and εἰνάτερες equations are recalled, not slab mappings
drift_or_renewal: Gk εἰνάτερες (*h₁yenh₂ter-, husband's brothers' wives) has no counterpart in this Russian list (Slavic keeps the word, ORuss. ятры/ятровь, but the song has тетушки instead); Vedic renews 'husband's sister' with nánāndṛ-
shared_syntax: a list (co-ordinated with да ... да / ἢ ... ἢ / Ved. uta) of the husband's kin terms, each a separate member, as the people the incoming wife must face; Gk and Vuk add the comparison 'father-in-law as (one's own) father' (ἑκυρὸς δὲ πατὴρ ὣς; свекра к'о свога бабајка)
context: All are the young wife's view of her husband's household: the Russian song (bride given away 'на чужую сторону') runs through свекор, свекруха, деверья, золовушки, each then reproaching her as she arrives; Helen (Il. 24.768-772) lists brothers-in-law, sisters-in-law, sisters-in-law by marriage and mother-in-law who reproached her, with the father-in-law always kind; the Vedic wedding verse makes the bride queen over the same set; Vuk 22086 tells the bride to treat the same set as her own kin. Same speaker position, same set of cognate terms, same theme of the in-laws' attitude to the incoming wife.
phrase: enumeration of the husband's kin (*swéḱuros, *sweḱrúh₂, *dayh₂wḗr, *ǵl̥h₂ōws) as the incoming wife's judges/subjects
note: The kin terms themselves and patrilocal marriage are inherited, so the list could arise independently wherever the terms survive; what goes beyond that is the shared speaker position, the reproach/kindness theme and the 'father-in-law as father' comparison in Gk and Serbian. Russian lyric song and Vuk are late oral traditions.

near_miss.lead: cast/fix the eyes (*h₃ekʷ-) to the earth (*dʰéǵʰōm): Russ. очи утупила во сыру землю ~ Gk κατὰ χθονὸς ὄμματα πήξας (Il. 3.217, not in slab)
near_miss.why_not: The slab's Greek partners (Od. 22.86, 22.94) are a man falling face first, not looking down; the true Greek parallel Il. 3.217 is a single line, and downcast eyes is a universal gesture of shame or thought with the most basic words for 'eye' and 'earth'.

near_miss.lead: sweet mead/honey: Russ. мед сладкий ~ Latv. medus saldums (*médʰu + BSl *sal-d- 'sweet')
near_miss.why_not: Honey is sweet in every language; the drift of *sal-d- to 'sweet' is a shared Balto-Slavic lexical innovation, so the pair proves nothing beyond Balto-Slavic vocabulary. The PIE adjective *swéh₂du- with honey (Ved. svādú/mádhu, 6 co-occurrences; Gk μελιηδής) is not renewed here in a matching context. The Latin partner (Cato Agr. 156) is a recipe with sal 'salt'.
Plain kin-term lists in a law, a charm and a letter; no shared context or figure.

near_miss.lead: smoke rolls: Russ. дым валит ~ Lat. uoluit ... fumum (*welH- 'roll' + *dʰuh₂mós)
near_miss.why_not: Common in byliny (12+ hits) but only one Latin hit (Lucretius on Etna, transitive), none elsewhere; 'rolling/billowing smoke' is a natural image (cf. English), so chance cannot be excluded.

near_miss.lead: dark night with *mergʷ-: Serb. ноћи ... мрака, мркла ноћ (Vuk 33208:10) ~ ON myrkt af nótt, nótt er myrk
near_miss.why_not: Night is dark everywhere; *mergʷ- is just the regional word for 'dark' in Germanic and Slavic; ON hits are saga prose.

near_miss.lead: wind blows (*h₂weh₁- verb with derived noun): Russ. повеют ветры ~ Skt vavau pavanaḥ
near_miss.why_not: The Sanskrit noun is pavana-, not vāta-; 'the wind blows' with root and derived noun is everyday language.

near_miss.lead: hot tears: Russ. горячи слезы (cf. Gk δάκρυα θερμά, Homer)
near_miss.why_not: AV partner is about ghee, not tears; 'hot tears' is a universal image and 'tear' itself is not cognate (слеза vs δάκρυ).
AV partner has only 'by nights'; the time formula is widespread (biblical too).

near_miss.lead: polyptoton hill to hill: Russ. с холмы на холму ~ Lat. colles collibus
near_miss.why_not: холм is a loan from Germanic (ON holmr); 'from X to X' polyptoton is generic and the Latin is an echo described in physics.

near_miss.lead: warm spring: Russ. теплая весна ~ Lat. uer ... tepores (*wósr̥ + *tep-)
near_miss.why_not: Spring is warm by definition; only 2 Slavic and 1 Latin co-occurrences in the corpora; no shared figure.
Generic; the star word is Balto-Slavic only.
Generic list of wild animals; the Slavic fox word is not cognate with ἀλώπηξ (see error line).

near_miss.lead: lie down and sleep at night (*legʰ- + *swep- + *nókʷts)
near_miss.why_not: Everyday narrative language in byliny and saga prose.

near_miss.lead: where the hero's horse's hooves strike, springs arise (cf. Hippocrene)
near_miss.why_not: The AV goat treading with pure hooves is not congruent; the Greek Hippocrene story uses non-cognate words and is not in the slab; копыто is better taken from копать than from *ḱoph₂ó-.
ON partner is a description of a giant's strength with no shared wording.
